\section{Introduction}

Fermionic Gaussian states, also known as quasifree or free-fermionic
states, constitute a central class of quantum states in many-body physics.
They arise naturally as ground states and thermal states of quadratic, and
hence noninteracting, fermionic Hamiltonians.  Remarkably, their reduced
states, entropies, and correlation functions can all be efficiently determined
from one-particle data, making them one of the paradigmatic exactly tractable
classes of quantum many-body states.  In a Majorana representation, these data
are encoded in the Majorana covariance matrix, denoted throughout this work

by
\(M\); equivalently, one may use the one-particle Green operator
\(G=(\one+iM)/2\).  The covariance description is classical in the theory of
quasifree states and is also central in fermionic linear optics and in the
analysis of free lattice models
\citep{ArakiQuasifree,BravyiFLO,TerhalDiVincenzo,Peschel2003,PeschelEisler2009}.
At the same time, fermionic Gaussian states are not merely a technical toy
model.  They include physically important examples with Fermi surfaces and
characteristic entanglement behaviour, including logarithmic violations of
entropic area laws
\citep{WolfAreaViolation,GioevKlich,EisertCramerPlenio,SwingleFermiSurface}.
They therefore provide a useful setting in which to test general ideas about
correlation, locality, exchangeability, and approximation in many-body quantum
systems.

One particularly important idea is mean-field theory.  Its basic
premise is that, when the influence on a local degree of freedom is distributed
among sufficiently many other degrees of freedom, the correlations carried by
any individual interaction become weak and a low-complexity variational
description becomes accurate.  In fermionic many-body theory, Hartree--Fock
theory is the canonical realization of this premise: one optimizes over Slater
determinants, or more generally over quasifree states when pairing is allowed,
thereby replacing an interacting problem by a self-consistent one-particle
description.  The setting of the present work is narrower but also more
quantitative.  We remain within the Gaussian class and ask when high
connectivity, symmetric extendibility, or spatial separation rigorously forces
an approximation by an even simpler Gaussian state, such as a product of local
marginals.  Thus, our product-state bounds should be understood as rigorous
Gaussian mean-field statements, closely related in spirit to Hartree--Fock but
not as an analysis of the full Hartree--Fock variational problem for interacting
fermions.

Motivated by this line of thought, the guiding question of this work is
when a fermionic Gaussian state can, for a given purpose, be replaced by a
simpler state.  We consider three precise versions of this question.  The first
is variational: when, and under what conditions, are the energy and free energy
of a quadratic fermionic Hamiltonian well approximated by product states?  The
second concerns exchangeability: when does the existence of many symmetric
extensions force a Gaussian state to be close to an independent product state?
The third is spatial and information-theoretic: when does a buffer region make
two distant regions approximately conditionally independent, so that the state
is approximately recoverable from one side of the buffer?  Although these
questions are usually treated by different methods, we show that in the
fermionic Gaussian setting they are governed by a common covariance-level
mechanism.

The starting point is the admissibility condition for Majorana covariance
matrices.  Informally, not every real antisymmetric matrix can be the
covariance matrix of a fermionic state: it must satisfy a positivity condition,
equivalently its singular values must be bounded by one.  This elementary
constraint has strong consequences for the way two-point correlations can be
distributed.  If a region \(A\) is correlated with many disjoint regions
\(B_1,\ldots,B_k\), then the covariance blocks from \(A\) to these regions
cannot all be large.  We refer to this as covariance monogamy.  The main point
of {this work

is that covariance monogamy, combined either with high degree,
exchangeability, or spatial separation, leads to quantitative approximation
theorems.

The first application concerns product-state approximations for high-degree
Hamiltonians.  For general two-local qudit Hamiltonians, Brand\~ao and Harrow
proved that high degree in the interaction graph forces the ground-state energy
to be well approximated by product states
\citep{BrandaoHarrowGround,BrandaoHarrowStates}.  Their result is based on
information-theoretic monogamy and applies far beyond the fermionic setting.
For quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians, however, the energy of an edge is
determined only by the two-point covariance block across that edge.  This makes
it possible to bypass dimension-dependent many-body approximation theorems and
work directly with covariance matrices.  In this way we obtain an
\(O(D^{-1/2})\) product-state approximation for quadratic Hamiltonians on
finite simple \(D\)-regular graphs.  If each site contains \(m\) fermionic
modes and the edge
terms are normalized in the high-degree convention, then there exists a product
state \(\varphi\) such that
\begin{equation}
        \tr(H\varphi)
        \le
        e_0(H)+\sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}}.
\end{equation}
The same argument gives the corresponding finite-temperature statement:
for a quadratic Hamiltonian, the product of the one-site marginals of the Gibbs
state has free energy within \(O(D^{-1/2})\) of the Gibbs variational optimum.
This result directly develops and substantially extends the program initiated in our earlier work
\citep{KrumnowZimborasEisertGroundApprox}.  That work established rigorous
Gaussian product-state approximations for general interacting fermionic
Hamiltonians from the weighted interaction graph and interpreted the underlying
correlation constraint as a non-symmetric fermionic de Finetti phenomenon.  The
present high-degree theorem retains the central idea that a local fermionic
degree of freedom cannot sustain strong correlations with many neighbours, but
specializes it to quadratic Hamiltonians, where every edge energy is exactly
determined by a two-point covariance block.  This extra structure replaces the
general many-body approximation argument by a direct covariance-budget estimate
and yields the sharper \(D^{-1/2}\) scaling.  The finite-temperature extension,
the exchangeable Gaussian de Finetti theorem below, and the approximate-Markov
result have no counterparts in Ref.~\citep{KrumnowZimborasEisertGroundApprox}.

The second application is a fermionic Gaussian de Finetti theorem.
Classical and quantum de Finetti theorems make precise the link between
extendibility and mean-field structure: permutation symmetry together with
extensions to arbitrarily many copies forces a state to be a mixture of
independent and identically distributed product states, while finite
extendibility yields quantitative approximations of this form.  This principle
has become a fundamental tool in quantum information theory, entanglement
theory, and rigorous mean-field analysis
\citep{Sturmer,HudsonMoody,ChristandlKoenigMitchisonRenner,RennerNatPhys,
BrandaoHarrowLocalMeasurements,LiSmith,RougerieDeFinetti}.  Fermionic systems
require additional care, because tensor-product language must be reconciled
with mode decompositions, anticommutation relations, and parity
superselection \citep{Negari_2026}.  These issues lead to several reasonable notions of fermionic
separability and mode entanglement
\citep{SchuchVerstraeteCiracFermions,BanulsCiracWolfFermionicEntanglement,
SpeeSchwaigerGiedkeKraus}.  They also motivate fermionic versions of de Finetti
theorems, such as the finite Majorana de Finetti theorem of Krumnow,
Zimbor\'as, and Eisert \citep{KrumnowZimborasEisert}.  Complementary fermionic
Gaussian de Finetti theorems based on Gaussian symmetry in the
matchgate-replica representation have recently been obtained, including an
exponential almost-i.i.d. version
\citep{SierantTurkeshiTarabungaMatchgateCommutant,
BurkatStudzinskiStrelchukExponentialDeFinetti}.

That said, our de Finetti result concerns a different setting.  It is restricted to
joint states that are themselves fermionic Gaussian and are extendible under
graded fermionic copy permutations, but within that setting it is completely
covariance-theoretic.  If a \(k\)-copy fermionic Gaussian state admits an
extension to \(n\) copies invariant under graded fermionic copy permutations,
then this symmetry forces all off-diagonal copy-copy covariance blocks to be
identical.
Admissibility of the \(n\)-copy covariance matrix then forces this common block
to be of order \(1/n\).  Converting the resulting covariance estimate into
trace norm, using perturbation bounds for free-fermionic states
\citep{BittelMeleEisertLeoneTraceDistance}, gives
\begin{equation}
        \left\|
        \rho_{A_1\cdots A_k}-\rho_A^{\otimes k}
        \right\|_1
        \le
        \frac{4m_A(k-1)}{n},
\end{equation}
where \(m_A\) is the number of fermionic modes in one copy.  Thus the
approximating de Finetti measure may be chosen to be the point mass at the
one-copy marginal.  In particular, an infinitely exchangeable fermionic
Gaussian state is exactly a product state.

The de Finetti result should also be compared with the recent work of
Negari and Salek \citep{NegariSalekExtendibility}.  There, the focus was on
two-sided \((k_1,k_2)\)-extendibility of bipartite fermionic Gaussian states,
its covariance-matrix characterization, and its consequences for approximation
by fermionic separable states.  The present work uses the same
covariance-matrix viewpoint and notation, but addresses a different
exchangeability problem: rather than approximating a bipartite extendible state
by the convex set of separable states, we study graded-permutation-invariant
extensions across many identical copies and prove closeness to the specific
product of the one-copy marginal.  Thus, the finite de Finetti theorem here is
an i.i.d. statement, with an explicit \(O(k/n)\) trace-norm bound, rather than a
separability statement.

Throughout this work, product and separability statements are understood with
respect to a fixed partition of fermionic modes, and all Gaussian states are
taken to be even.  For Gaussian states this convention has a simple covariance
interpretation: the product of the Gaussian marginals on disjoint regions is
obtained by deleting the off-diagonal covariance blocks between the regions.
This is the convention used in \citep{NegariSalekExtendibility}, and it is
consistent with the mode-based treatment of fermionic entanglement under parity
superselection
\citep{SchuchVerstraeteCiracFermions,BanulsCiracWolfFermionicEntanglement,
SpeeSchwaigerGiedkeKraus}.  The preliminaries section below recalls the precise
operator-algebraic and covariance-matrix conventions used in the proofs.

The third application concerns conditional mutual information and approximate
Markov structure.  For a tripartite state on \(A,B,C\), the conditional mutual
information
\begin{equation}
        I(A:C\mid B)
        =
        S(A,B)+S(B,C)-S(B)-S(A,B,C)
\end{equation}
measures the part of the correlation between \(A\) and \(C\) that remains after
the degrees of freedom in \(B\) have been retained.  Exact vanishing of this
quantity characterizes quantum Markov chains
\citep{HaydenJozsaPetzWinter,IbinsonLindenWinter}; quantitatively, the
Fawzi--Renner recoverability theorem and its refinements show that small
conditional mutual information implies approximate recovery by a quantum
channel acting on the conditioning system
\citep{FawziRenner,SutterTomamichelHarrow,JungeRennerSutterWildeWinter,
WildeRecoverability}.

Approximate Markov structure has become an important locality concept in
quantum many-body theory \citep{,negari2026criticalnonequilibriumphasesnoisy,kumar2026unlearnablephasesmatter}.  It is closely related to Gibbs-state locality,
Markov networks, and the locality of entanglement spectra
\citep{PoulinHastingsMarkov,KimConditionalIndependence,KatoBrandao,
KuwaharaKatoBrandao,KatoBrandaoEdge}.  Recent work has further clarified the
decay of conditional mutual information in thermal and many-body settings
\citep{kuwahara2024clusteringconditional,kato2025clusteringconditionalmutual}.
However, conditional mutual information is not controlled by ordinary
correlation decay in a purely formal way: conditioning can remove correlations,
but it can also create them.  This makes the question of conditional
independence across a spatial buffer genuinely different from the decay of
ordinary two-point functions or even from the decay of mutual information.

Fermionic Gaussian states again provide a rigid setting in which this question
can be attacked directly.  Entropies of reduced Gaussian states are trace
functions of compressed one-particle Green operators.  This permits an
expansion of the conditional mutual information in terms of powers of the
compressed Green operators.  If the state has exponentially clustering mutual
information, then for fixed finite regions this is equivalent, up to constants
and decay rates, to exponential decay of the corresponding off-diagonal
one-particle blocks; this is the Gaussian analogue of the connection between
information clustering and correlation decay studied in other many-body
settings
\citep{wolf2007arealawsquantumsystems,bluhm2021exponentialdecaymutualinformation}.
Using the trace expansion, we show that the Green-function paths connecting
two outer regions through a growing buffer give a summable contribution.  As a
result, for disjoint translates \(A\) and \(C\) of fixed finite reference
shapes \(A_0\) and \(C_0\), separated by a buffer \(B_r\), we prove
\begin{equation}
        I_\rho(A:C\mid B_r)
        \le
        \frac{K_{A_0,C_0,\rho}}{r},
\end{equation}
where the constant is independent of the buffer scale \(r\).  The
Fawzi--Renner theorem then gives
\begin{equation}
        \inf_{\mathcal R_{B_r\to B_r C}}
        \left\|
        \rho_{A,B_r,C}
        -
        (\id_A\otimes\mathcal R_{B_r\to B_r ,C})(\rho_{A,B_r})
        \right\|_1
        =
        O(r^{-1/2}).
\end{equation}
Thus spatial clustering at the one-particle level yields an approximate-recovery
description for fermionic Gaussian states.

The three approximation results are logically independent, but they share a
common mechanism.  High degree spreads a finite covariance budget over many
interaction edges.  Exchangeability forces all copy-copy covariance blocks to
be identical, and admissibility then makes each of them small.  Spatial
clustering suppresses the covariance paths that contribute to conditional
mutual information across a buffer.  In all three cases, a many-body
approximation statement is obtained by first proving a one-particle covariance
estimate and then converting it into the relevant variational or
information-theoretic quantity.

The remainder of this work is organized as follows.  Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} fixes the
fermionic covariance-matrix notation, including Majorana covariance matrices,
Gaussian states, the Green operator, and the entropy formula.  Section~\ref{sec:highdegree}
proves covariance monogamy and applies it to product-state approximations for
quadratic Hamiltonians on high-degree graphs, both at zero and positive
temperature.  Section~\ref{sec:definetti} proves the finite fermionic Gaussian
de Finetti theorem and the infinite-exchangeability corollary.  Section~\ref{sec:markov}
proves the conditional mutual information bound for spatially clustering
fermionic Gaussian states and derives the corresponding recoverability
estimate.  Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses possible refinements and
extensions.

\section{Preliminaries}\label{sec:preliminaries}

We collect the notation and basic facts about fermionic Gaussian states that
will be used throughout this work.  All systems considered here contain finitely
many fermionic modes unless explicitly stated otherwise.  For an operator
\(X\), we write
\begin{equation}
        \|X\|_p
        =
        \bigl(\tr (X^\dagger X)^{p/2}\bigr)^{1/p},
        \qquad 1\le p<\infty ,
\end{equation}
for the Schatten \(p\)-norm, and \(\|X\|_\infty\) for the operator norm.  For
Hermitian matrices \(A,B\), the notation \(A\succeq0\) means that \(A\) is
positive semidefinite, and \(A\preceq B\) means \(B-A\succeq0\).

\subsection{Fermionic modes, parity, and local regions}

We begin by fixing the operator-algebraic conventions that determine
locality, parity, and signs throughout the covariance-matrix analysis.
An \(m\)-mode fermionic system is described by creation and annihilation
operators
$
        c_1^\dagger,\ldots,c_m^\dagger$ and
        $c_1,\ldots,c_m $,
satisfying the canonical anticommutation relations
\begin{equation}\label{eq:CAR}
        \{c_j,c_k^\dagger\}=\delta_{j,k}\one,
        \qquad
        \{c_j,c_k\}=\{c_j^\dagger,c_k^\dagger\}=0 
\end{equation}
for $j,k=1,\dots, m$.
The Hilbert space is the fermionic Fock space
\(\mathcal F_m\cong(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m}\), after choosing a fixed global
ordering of the modes.  This ordering is part of the convention: fermionic
operators supported on disjoint mode sets anticommute before passing to the
even local algebras, and therefore signs in covariance blocks depend on the
chosen global order.
The number operator and parity operator are given by
\begin{equation}
        \widehat N=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j^\dagger c_j,
        \qquad
        P=(-1)^{\widehat N}.
\end{equation}
Physical fermionic states obey the parity superselection rule
\begin{equation}\label{eq:parity-superselection}
        [\rho,P]=0 .
\end{equation}
Equivalently, a physical state is block diagonal with respect to the even and
odd parity sectors.  In particular, expectations of odd monomials in the
fermionic field operators vanish.  Throughout this work, 
all Gaussian states
are understood to be even, hence physical in this sense. 
Number-conserving fermionic states additionally commute with the total particle-number operator.

If \(A\) is a finite set of modes, we denote by \(m_A\) the number of
fermionic modes in \(A\).  The associated real Majorana one-particle space has
dimension
\begin{equation}
        N_A:=2m_A .
\end{equation}
We reserve the symbol \(M_A\) for the covariance matrix of the subsystem
\(A\), and use \(N_A\) for the Majorana one-particle dimension.  The projection
onto the Majorana one-particle space of \(A\) is denoted by \(\Pi_A\).

\subsection{Majorana operators and covariance matrices}

We next express the fermionic operators through Majorana modes and fix the covariance sign convention used in the proofs.
From the creation and annihilation operators we define Hermitian Majorana
operators by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:majorana-definition}
        \gamma_{2j-1}=c_j+c_j^\dagger,
        \qquad
        \gamma_{2j}=i(c_j-c_j^\dagger),
        \qquad j=1,\ldots,m .
\end{equation}
They satisfy the Clifford relations
\begin{equation}\label{eq:majorana-CAR}
        \{\gamma_p,\gamma_q\}=2\delta_{p,q}\one,
        \qquad
        \gamma_p^\dagger=\gamma_p .
\end{equation}
With the convention \eqref{eq:majorana-definition}, the parity operator may be
written as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:parity-majorana}
        P
        =
        (-i)^m\prod_{j=1}^m \gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}.
\end{equation}

For a physical state \(\rho\), its Majorana covariance matrix, abbreviated
CM, is the real antisymmetric matrix \(M\in\mathbb R^{2m\times2m}\) defined by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:majorana-covariance}
        M_{p,q}
        :=
        \frac{i}{2}\tr\!\left(\rho[\gamma_q,\gamma_p]\right)
        =
        \begin{cases}      \tr\!\left(i\gamma_q\gamma_p\rho\right), & p\ne q,\\[1mm]
        0, & p=q .
        \end{cases}
\end{equation}
This is the sign convention used in Ref.~\citep{NegariSalekExtendibility}.  Notice
in particular that, for \(p\ne q\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-point-from-M}
        \tr(\rho\,\gamma_p\gamma_q)
        =
        iM_{p,q}.
\end{equation}
A matrix \(M\) is a valid fermionic covariance matrix if and only if it is real
antisymmetric and satisfies the bona fide condition
\begin{equation}\label{eq:covariance-positivity}
        \one+iM\succeq0 .
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the eigenvalues of the Hermitian matrix \(iM\) lie in
\([-1,1]\), or, equivalently, all singular values of \(M\) are at most one.
Thus there exists an orthogonal matrix \(O\in SO(2m)\) and real numbers
\(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\in[-1,1]\) such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:canonical-form-M}
        M
        =
        O
        \left(
        \bigoplus_{j=1}^m
        \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & \lambda_j\\
        -\lambda_j & 0
        \end{pmatrix}
        \right)
        O^T .
\end{equation}
For a pure Gaussian state one has \(M^2=-\one\), equivalently
\(|\lambda_j|=1\) for every \(j\).
For a general physical state, the covariance matrix records only the second
moments.  For a fermionic Gaussian state, however, the covariance matrix
determines the state completely.

\subsection{Fermionic Gaussian states}

We now turn to our main object of study, multi-mode Gaussian states.
A parity-preserving state \(\rho\) is called fermionic Gaussian if it can be
written, up to normalization, as the exponential of a quadratic form in
Majorana operators,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gaussian-exponential}
        \rho
        =
        Z^{-1}
        \exp\!\left(
        \frac{i}{2}\sum_{p,q} h_{p,q}\gamma_p\gamma_q
        \right),
        \qquad
        h=-h^T\in\mathbb R^{2m\times2m},
\end{equation}
with the usual limiting interpretation for pure states.  Equivalently, a state
is Gaussian if and only if all of its higher-order correlations are determined
by its two-point correlations through Wick's rule.  Odd Majorana moments vanish,
and every even Majorana moment is given by the Pfaffian of the corresponding
two-point matrix.

Conversely, every real antisymmetric matrix \(M\) satisfying
\eqref{eq:covariance-positivity} is the covariance matrix of a unique even
fermionic Gaussian state.  We denote this state by \(\rho_M\).  Thus, within
the Gaussian class,
\begin{equation}
        M
        \longleftrightarrow
        \rho_M,
\end{equation}
is a one-to-one parametrization.
We shall use the following covariance-to-state continuity estimate for
fermionic Gaussian states~\citep{BittelMeleEisertLeoneTraceDistance}.  If \(M\) and \(M'\) 
are two valid covariance
matrices, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gaussian-covariance-lipschitz-prelim}
        \|\rho_M-\rho_{M'}\|_1
        \le
        \frac12\|M-M'\|_1 .
\end{equation}
This bound allows covariance estimates to be converted directly into
trace-norm estimates for Gaussian states.

\subsection{Restrictions, block structure, and Gaussian product states}

We describe how covariance matrices restrict to regions and how their off-diagonal blocks quantify the failure of Gaussian states to factorize.
The covariance formalism is compatible with restriction to subsystems.  
If
\(A\) is a finite region, then the reduced state \(\rho_A\) of a Gaussian state
\(\rho_M\) is Gaussian with covariance matrix
\begin{equation}\label{eq:restricted-covariance}
        M_A
        =
        \Pi_A M\Pi_A .
\end{equation}
More generally, for two disjoint regions \(A\) and \(B\), written in the
global ordering where the modes of \(A\) precede the modes of \(B\), the
covariance matrix has the block form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-covariance}
        M_{A,B}
        =
        \begin{pmatrix}
        M_A & X_{A,B}\\
        -X_{A,B}^T & M_B
        \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Here
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cross-covariance-block}
        X_{A,B}:=\Pi_A M\Pi_B,
\end{equation}
is the covariance block across the cut \(A|B\).  With the convention
\eqref{eq:majorana-covariance}, if \(a\) labels a Majorana mode in \(A\) and
\(b\) labels a Majorana mode in \(B\), then
\begin{equation}
        (X_{A,B})_{a,b}
        =
        \tr\!\left(i\gamma_b\gamma_a\rho\right).
\end{equation}
For disjoint regions \(A,B_1,\ldots,B_k\), we shall often write
\begin{equation}
        X_i:=
        X_{A, B_i}.
\end{equation}

The product of the Gaussian marginals on \(A\) and \(B\) is the Gaussian state
with covariance matrix
\begin{equation}\label{eq:product-covariance}
        M_A\oplus M_B .
\end{equation}
Thus, in the Gaussian setting, passing from a joint state to the product of
its Gaussian marginals is exactly the operation of deleting the off-diagonal
covariance block \(X_{A,B}\).  In particular,
\begin{equation}
        X_{A,B}=0
        \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
        \rho_{M_{A,B}}=\rho_{M_A}\otimes\rho_{M_B},
\end{equation}
for Gaussian states, with the tensor product understood with respect to the
fixed global mode ordering.

The sign convention in \eqref{eq:majorana-covariance} is relevant when writing
expectations of oriented quadratic Hamiltonian terms.  If
\begin{equation}
        H_{A,B}
        =
        i\bm\gamma_A^T K_{A,B}\bm\gamma_B,
        \qquad
        K_{A,B}\in\mathbb R^{N_A\times N_B},
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-expectation-M}
        \tr(\rho H_{A,B})
        =
        -\tr(K_{A,B}^T X_{A,B}).
\end{equation}
The sign can of course be absorbed into the definition of the oriented
coupling matrix \(K_{A,B}\), and the estimates in this work use only the
absolute value of this pairing.

\subsection{Majorana Green operator and entropy}

The final preliminary connects the covariance matrix to entropy, preparing the conditional mutual-information argument below.
For entropy estimates it is convenient to use the one-particle operator
associated with the covariance matrix.  Given a valid covariance matrix \(M\),
define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:green-definition}
        G
        :=
        \frac{\one+iM}{2}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
        0\preceq G\preceq\one,
        \qquad
        G^\dagger=G,
        \qquad
        M=-i(2G-\one).
\end{equation}
Since \(M\) is real and antisymmetric, \(G\) also satisfies the particle-hole
symmetry
\begin{equation}\label{eq:particle-hole-G}
        G^T=\one-G .
\end{equation}
For a finite region \(A\), we write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:restricted-G}
        G_A
        :=
        \Pi_A G\Pi_A .
\end{equation}
If \(A\) contains \(m_A\) fermionic modes, then
\begin{equation}
        \rank\Pi_A=N_A=2m_A,
        \qquad
        \tr G_A=m_A .
\end{equation}
The entropy of the reduced Gaussian state \(\rho_A\) is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:entropy-green}
        S(\rho_A)
        =
        -\tr\bigl(G_A\log G_A\bigr),
\end{equation}
where the trace is taken over the Majorana one-particle space of \(A\).  The
particle-hole symmetry \eqref{eq:particle-hole-G} ensures that this expression
counts each physical fermionic mode correctly: the eigenvalues of \(G_A\) come
in pairs \(\lambda,1-\lambda\).

For two finite regions \(A\) and \(B\), we also use the block notation
\begin{equation}
        G_{A,B}:=\Pi_A G\Pi_B .
\end{equation}
In spatial sections, when \(x,y\) are lattice sites or finite cells,
\(G_{x, y}\) denotes the corresponding one-particle block from the Majorana
space over \(y\) to the Majorana space over \(x\).  Thus \(G_X\) is the
compression of \(G\) to \(X\), whereas \(G_{x, y}\) is the off-diagonal block
between the sites \(x\) and \(y\).

\section{Product-state approximation on high-degree graphs}
\label{sec:highdegree}

A central problem in many-body theory is to identify variational classes that
approximate ground-state energies without requiring a description of the full
many-body state.  Product states are the simplest possible ansatz.  For a
general local Hamiltonian, however, there is no reason for such an ansatz to be
accurate: local interactions may create entanglement on many edges, and the
ground-state energy can depend essentially on these correlations.  It is
therefore important to understand regimes in which the variational problem
simplifies and product states become approximately optimal.

One such regime is the dense, or high-degree, interaction-graph limit.  If each
local system interacts with many others, then in the normalized Hamiltonian the
contribution of any single edge is small in the global energy.  Brand\~ao and
Harrow \citep{BrandaoHarrowGround,BrandaoHarrowStates} have made this principle
quantitative for general qudit Hamiltonians: for local dimension
\(d_{\rm loc}\), the product-state approximation error scales as
\begin{equation}
        \left(\frac{d_{\rm loc}^2\log d_{\rm loc}}{D}\right)^{1/3},
\end{equation}
where \(D\) is the degree of the interaction graph.

The purpose of this section is to prove a substantially sharper version of this phenomenon
for quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians.  The improvement comes from the
covariance-matrix structure 
of fermionic systems.  For a quadratic fermionic
interaction, the energy of an edge is determined entirely by the two-point
Majorana covariance block across that edge. We show that a fixed fermionic
region can share only a bounded total amount of two-point covariance with many
disjoint regions.  Thus, on a high-degree graph, the average covariance across
an interaction edge is small.  This gives a product-state approximation with
error scaling as
\begin{equation}
        \left(\frac{\log d_{\rm loc}}{D}\right)^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the dependence on \(d_{\rm loc}\) improves from polynomial to
polylogarithmic, while the dependence on the degree improves from \(D^{-1/3}\)
to \(D^{-1/2}\).

Conceptually, this is the exactly quadratic counterpart of the interacting
fermionic approximation theorem in our earlier work
\citep{KrumnowZimborasEisertGroundApprox}: the same obstruction to distributing
fermionic correlations is used here at the covariance level, where it yields a
stronger rate and a substantially shorter argument.
We use the high-degree normalization of Brand\~ao and Harrow
\citep{BrandaoHarrowGround,BrandaoHarrowStates}.  Let
\(\mathcal G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple \(D\)-regular graph, with \(D\ge1\),
on \(n=|V|\) vertices.  In particular, the graph has neither loops nor
parallel edges.  The
vertices label local systems \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_n\), each of local dimension
\(d_{\rm loc}\), and the edges specify the two-body interactions.  We write the
Hamiltonian as the edge average
\begin{equation}
        H
        =
        \mathbb E_{(i,j)\in E} H_{i,j}
        =
        \frac{2}{nD}\sum_{(i,j)\in E} H_{i,j},
        \label{eq:BH-normalized-H}
\end{equation}
where \(H_{i,j}\) is supported on \(Q_i\cup Q_j\), and
\(\|H_{i,j}\|\le 1\) for every edge.  With this convention,
\(\tr(H\rho)\) is an intensive energy and the local interaction terms obey a
degree-independent operator-norm bound.

We now restrict to the quadratic fermionic case.  Each \(Q_i\) is the Fock
space of \(m\) fermionic modes, so that
$ d_{\rm loc}=2^m $.
Let
\begin{equation}
        \bm\gamma_i
        =
        (\gamma_{i,1},\ldots,\gamma_{i,2m})^T,
\end{equation}
denote the vector of Majorana operators at vertex \(i\).  After fixing an
arbitrary orientation of each edge, we write the inter-site interaction as
\begin{equation}
        H_{i,j}
        =
        i\bm\gamma_i^T K_{i,j}\bm\gamma_j,
        \qquad
        K_{i,j}\in\mathbb R^{2m\times 2m}.
        \label{eq:fermionic-edge-Hij}
\end{equation}
Here the factor of \(i\) makes the operator self-adjoint, since Majorana
operators on distinct sites anticommute.  The chosen orientation is only a
bookkeeping convention for writing \(K_{i,j}\); the estimates below depend only
on norms and are independent of this choice.

To proceed, let
\begin{equation}
        e_0(H)
        :=
        \min_{\rho}\tr(H\rho)
        \label{eq:ground-energy-definition},
\end{equation}
be the ground-state energy.  The high-degree product approximation for
quadratic fermions is the following.
Here and below, variational optimizations are over physical parity-preserving
fermionic states.

\begin{theorem}[High-degree product approximation for quadratic fermions]
\label{thm:fermionic-product-state-approximation}
Let \(\mathcal G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple \(D\)-regular graph, with
\(D\ge1\), on \(n\) vertices, and let
\(H\) be a quadratic fermionic Hamiltonian of the form
\eqref{eq:BH-normalized-H}--\eqref{eq:fermionic-edge-Hij}.  Assume that
\(\|H_{i,j}\|\le 1\) for every \((i,j)\in E\).  Then there exists a physical
product state
\begin{equation}
        \varphi
        =
        \varphi^{Q_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\varphi^{Q_n},
\end{equation}
such that
\begin{equation}
        \tr(H\varphi)
        \le
        e_0(H)
        +
        \sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}}
        =
        e_0(H)
        +
        \sqrt{\frac{2\log_2 d_{\rm loc}}{D}} .
        \label{eq:fermionic-product-state-bound}
\end{equation}
In fact, each factor of \(\varphi\) may be chosen as a pure parity eigenstate.
\end{theorem}

The proof isolates the genuinely fermionic input in a covariance monogamy
bound.  This bound is not a property of the Hamiltonian and does not require
Gaussianity; it follows from the admissibility condition for Majorana
covariance matrices.  Once this monogamy estimate is established, the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:fermionic-product-state-approximation} is direct: applying
the bound at each vertex controls the average covariance across an interaction
edge, and the quadratic form \eqref{eq:fermionic-edge-Hij} converts this
covariance estimate into an energy estimate.

\subsection{Covariance monogamy}
\label{subsec:covariance-monogamy}

The first ingredient is a monogamy bound for fermionic two-point correlations.
If one region \(A\) is correlated with many disjoint regions
\(B_1,\ldots,B_k\), then the covariance blocks from \(A\) to these regions
cannot all be large.  More precisely, the total covariance budget of \(A\) is
finite, and therefore the average two-point covariance between \(A\) and one of
the regions \(B_i\) goes to zero as the number of regions grows.

Let \(\rho\) be a physical fermionic state on \(A, B_1,\cdots ,B_k\), not
necessarily Gaussian. We can write its  
Majorana covariance matrix in block form as
\begin{equation}
M_{AB_1\cdots B_k}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
M_A & X_1 & X_2 & \cdots & X_k\\
-X_1^T & M_{B_1} & * & \cdots & *\\
-X_2^T & * & M_{B_2} & \cdots & *\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
-X_k^T & * & * & \cdots & M_{B_k}
\end{pmatrix}.
\label{eq:monogamy-block-form}
\end{equation}
Here
\begin{equation}
        X_i=\Pi_A M\Pi_{B_i},
\end{equation}
is the two-point covariance block between \(A\) and \(B_i\), and the starred
blocks denote covariance blocks among the regions \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\), which
will not be used.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp monogamy of fermionic two-point correlations]
\label{thm:monogamy}
Let \(A\) contain \(m_A\) fermionic modes.  Let \(\rho\) be a physical
fermionic state, not necessarily Gaussian, on disjoint regions
\(A,B_1,\dots,B_k\), and let \(M\) be its Majorana covariance matrix.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:opineq}
\sum_{i=1}^{k}X_iX_i^{T}\;\preceq\;\one_A ,
\end{equation}
and consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trineq}
\E_i\,\HS{X_i}^{2}
=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\HS{X_i}^{2}
\;\le\;\frac{2m_A}{k},
\end{equation}
where $i$ is chosen uniformly from $\{1,\dots,k\}$. Both bounds are optimal,
see Example~\ref{ex:sharp}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The projections $\Pi_{B_1},\dots,\Pi_{B_k}$ have mutually orthogonal ranges,
so $\Pi_B:=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Pi_{B_i}$ is the orthogonal projection onto the
Majorana one-particle space of $B:=B_1\cup\dots\cup B_k$, and
$\Pi_B\preceq\one$. Using $\Pi_{B_i}\Pi_{B_i}^{T}=\Pi_{B_i}$,
\begin{equation}
\sum_{i=1}^{k}X_iX_i^{T}
=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Pi_A M\Pi_{B_i}M^{T}\Pi_A
=\Pi_A M\,\Pi_B\,M^{T}\Pi_A
\;\preceq\;\Pi_A MM^{T}\Pi_A
\;\preceq\;\Pi_A ,
\end{equation}
where the first inequality is the congruence of $\Pi_B\preceq\one$ by $M$, and the second follows from $MM^{T}\preceq\one$. Restricting to the range of $\Pi_A$ yields \eqref{eq:opineq}. Taking the trace gives
\begin{equation}
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\HS{X_i}^{2}
=\tr\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{k}X_iX_i^{T}\Bigr)
\le\tr\Pi_A=N_A=2m_A ,
\end{equation}
and dividing by $k$ proves \eqref{eq:trineq}.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Optimality for every $k$]\label{ex:sharp}
Let each $B_i$ contain $m_A$ modes, and consider the real antisymmetric
matrix with vanishing diagonal and $B_iB_j$ blocks,
\begin{equation}
M=\begin{pmatrix}
0 & X_1 & \cdots & X_k\\
-X_1^{T} & 0 & \cdots & 0\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
-X_k^{T} & 0 & \cdots & 0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
X_i=k^{-1/2}\,\one_{N_A}.
\end{equation}
Then $MM^{T}=\one_{N_A}\oplus\bigl(\tfrac{1}{k}J_k\otimes\one_{N_A}\bigr)$,
where $J_k$ is the $k\times k$ all-ones matrix. Since $\tfrac1k J_k$ has
eigenvalues $1$ and $0$, we get
$\mathrm{spec}(MM^{T})\subset\{0,1\}$, so $\|M\|_{\infty}=1$ and $M$ is the covariance matrix of a unique fermionic Gaussian state. For this state,
\begin{equation}
\sum_{i=1}^{k}X_iX_i^{T}=\one_A,
\qquad
\HS{X_i}^{2}=\frac{N_A}{k}=\frac{2m_A}{k}
\quad\text{for every }i,
\end{equation}
so \eqref{eq:opineq} is saturated and \eqref{eq:trineq} holds with equality
termwise. Hence neither the operator bound, nor the constant $2m_A$, nor the
$1/k$ scaling can be improved.
\end{example}

\subsection{Proof of the product-state approximation}
\label{subsec:proof-product-approximation}

We now use the covariance monogamy bound to prove
Theorem~\ref{thm:fermionic-product-state-approximation}.  Since \(H\) is a
finite quadratic fermionic Hamiltonian, it has a fermionic Gaussian ground
state.  Choose such a ground state \(\rho_0\), so that
\begin{equation}
        \tr(H\rho_0)=e_0(H).
\end{equation}
For an oriented edge \((i,j)\in E\), let \(M^{(0)}\) be the covariance matrix
of \(\rho_0\), and define
\begin{equation}
        X_{i,j}^{(0)}
        :=
        \Pi_i M^{(0)}\Pi_j .
\end{equation}
Thus, with the convention of \eqref{eq:majorana-covariance},
\begin{equation}
        X_{i,j}^{(0)}(a,b)
        =
        \tr\!\left(i\gamma_{j,b}\gamma_{i,a}\rho_0\right).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
        \tr\!\left(\rho_0\,i\gamma_{i,a}\gamma_{j,b}\right)
        =
        -X_{i,j}^{(0)}(a,b).
\end{equation}
Since
\begin{equation}
        H_{i,j}
        =
        i\bm\gamma_i^T K_{i,j}\bm\gamma_j,
\end{equation}
we have
\begin{equation}
        \tr(\rho_0 H_{i,j})
        =
        -\tr\!\left(K_{i,j}^T X_{i,j}^{(0)}\right).
        \label{eq:edge-expectation-covariance}
\end{equation}

We first translate the operator normalization of \(H_{i,j}\) into the
one-particle bound needed for the covariance estimate.  Let \(s_\alpha\) be
the singular values of \(K_{i,j}\).  By applying orthogonal changes of
Majorana basis at the two endpoints, the edge term is brought to the form
\begin{equation}
        \sum_\alpha s_\alpha\, i\eta_\alpha\widetilde\eta_\alpha ,
\end{equation}
where the operators \(i\eta_\alpha\widetilde\eta_\alpha\) are commuting
self-adjoint involutions.  Hence
\begin{equation}
        \|H_{i,j}\|
        =
        \sum_\alpha s_\alpha
        =
        \|K_{i,j}\|_1 .
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
        \|K_{i,j}\|_2
        \le
        \|K_{i,j}\|_1
        =
        \|H_{i,j}\|
        \le
        1 .
\end{equation}
Therefore, by \eqref{eq:edge-expectation-covariance} and Cauchy--Schwarz,
\begin{equation}
        \left|\tr(\rho_0 H_{i,j})\right|
        =
        \left|\tr\!\left(K_{i,j}^T X_{i,j}^{(0)}\right)\right|
        \le
        \|K_{i,j}\|_2\,\|X_{i,j}^{(0)}\|_2
        \le
        \|X_{i,j}^{(0)}\|_2 .
        \label{eq:edge-energy-by-X}
\end{equation}

Now fix a vertex \(i\).  Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:monogamy} with
\(A=Q_i\) and with \(B_j=Q_j\) for \(j\in N(i)\), where \(N(i)\) denotes the
neighbourhood of \(i\), gives
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{j\in N(i)}
        \|\Pi_i M^{(0)}\Pi_j\|_2^2
        \le
        2m .
\end{equation}
Summing this estimate over all \(i\in V\) counts each undirected edge twice.
The two orientations give covariance blocks that differ only by a transpose
and a sign, and therefore have the same Hilbert--Schmidt norm.  Since
\(|E|=nD/2\), we obtain
\begin{equation}
        \mathbb E_{(i,j)\in E}
        \|X_{i,j}^{(0)}\|_2^2
        \le
        \frac{2m}{D}.
\end{equation}
Jensen's inequality then gives
\begin{equation}
        \mathbb E_{(i,j)\in E}
        \|X_{i,j}^{(0)}\|_2
        \le
        \sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}} .
        \label{eq:average-edge-X-bound}
\end{equation}

Let
\begin{equation}
        \sigma
        =
        \rho_0^{Q_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_0^{Q_n},
\end{equation}
be the product of the one-site marginals of \(\rho_0\).  At the covariance
level, passing from \(\rho_0\) to \(\sigma\) keeps all one-site covariance
blocks and deletes all covariance blocks between distinct sites.  Therefore,
for every edge \((i,j)\in E\), the covariance block of \(\sigma\) between
\(i\) and \(j\) is zero.  Using \eqref{eq:edge-expectation-covariance}, we get
\begin{equation}
        \tr(\sigma H_{i,j})-\tr(\rho_0 H_{i,j})
        =
        \tr\!\left(K_{i,j}^T X_{i,j}^{(0)}\right).
\end{equation}
Averaging over edges and using \eqref{eq:average-edge-X-bound}, we find
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
        \tr(H\sigma)-e_0(H)
        &=
        \mathbb E_{(i,j)\in E}
        \left[
        \tr(\sigma H_{i,j})-\tr(\rho_0 H_{i,j})
        \right]  \\
        &\le
        \mathbb E_{(i,j)\in E}
        \left|
        \tr\!\left(K_{i,j}^T X_{i,j}^{(0)}\right)
        \right|  \\
        &\le
        \mathbb E_{(i,j)\in E}
        \|X_{i,j}^{(0)}\|_2
        \le
        \sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}} .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Thus
\begin{equation}
        \tr(H\sigma)
        \le
        e_0(H)+\sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}} .
\end{equation}

The state \(\sigma\) is a product state, but it need not be pure.  Each
one-site marginal \(\rho_0^{Q_i}\) commutes with the corresponding local
parity operator and therefore admits a spectral decomposition into pure parity
eigenstates.  Consequently, \(\sigma\) is a convex combination of physical
pure product states.  The energy is affine in the state, so at least one such
pure product state
\begin{equation}
        \varphi
        =
        \varphi^{Q_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\varphi^{Q_n},
\end{equation}
in this decomposition satisfies
\begin{equation}
        \tr(H\varphi)\le \tr(H\sigma).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
        \tr(H\varphi)
        \le
        e_0(H)+\sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}}
        =
        e_0(H)+\sqrt{\frac{2\log_2 d_{\rm loc}}{D}} .
\end{equation}
This proves Theorem~\ref{thm:fermionic-product-state-approximation}.

\begin{remark}[On-site terms]
\label{rem:onsite-terms}
The theorem is stated for Hamiltonians whose edge terms are purely inter-site
quadratic fermionic interactions.  This is only for notational simplicity.  The
same conclusion holds if one adds arbitrary even on-site terms,
\begin{equation}
        H_{\rm loc}
        =
        \frac1n\sum_{i\in V} h_i,
\end{equation}
where each \(h_i\) is an even self-adjoint operator on \(Q_i\), equivalently
\([h_i,P_i]=0\), with \(P_i\) the local parity operator, but need not be
quadratic.  Indeed, in the proof above the approximating product state is
obtained by replacing a state \(\rho\) with the product of its
one-site marginals,
\begin{equation}
        \rho^{Q_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho^{Q_n}.
\end{equation}
This replacement preserves every one-site reduced state, and hence preserves
the expectation of \(H_{\rm loc}\).  The only terms whose expectation can
change are the inter-site quadratic terms, and these are exactly the terms
controlled by the covariance monogamy bound.  Thus the hypothesis needed for
the argument is not that the whole Hamiltonian be quadratic, but only that the
inter-site interactions along the graph are quadratic fermionic operators.
For the enlarged Hamiltonian one starts with any physical ground state;
Gaussianity is not needed because Theorem~\ref{thm:monogamy} applies to
arbitrary physical states.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Finite-temperature free energy}
\label{subsec:free-energy-product-approximation}

The covariance-monogamy mechanism is not confined to ground states.  It also
shows that the thermodynamic variational problem becomes effectively
mean-field-like on interaction graphs of high degree.  To make this precise,
let \(\beta>0\) denote the inverse temperature and define the free-energy
functional by

\begin{equation}
        F_\beta(\omega)
        =
        \tr(H\omega)-\beta^{-1}S(\omega),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
        S(\omega)=-\tr(\omega\log\omega),
\end{equation}
is the von Neumann entropy.  Here \(\beta\) is conjugate to the normalized,
intensive Hamiltonian \(H\).  Equivalently, with \(\widehat H=nH\) and
\(\beta_{\rm phys}=\beta/n\), the functional \(F_\beta\) is the physical free
energy per site for \((\widehat H,\beta_{\rm phys})\).  Let
\begin{equation}
        \rho_\beta
        =
        \frac{e^{-\beta H}}{\tr(e^{-\beta H})},
\end{equation}
be the Gibbs state of \(H\).  Since \(H\) is quadratic, \(\rho_\beta\) is a
fermionic Gaussian state.

\begin{theorem}[Fermionic Gaussian product approximation for free energy]
\label{thm:fermionic-free-energy-product}
Let \(\mathcal G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple \(D\)-regular graph, with
\(D\ge1\), on \(n\) vertices, and let
\(H\) be a quadratic fermionic Hamiltonian of the form
\eqref{eq:BH-normalized-H}--\eqref{eq:fermionic-edge-Hij}.  Assume that
\(\|H_{i,j}\|\le 1\) for every \((i,j)\in E\).  For \(\beta>0\), let
\(\rho_\beta\) be the Gibbs state of \(H\), and define the product of its
one-site marginals by
\begin{equation}
        \sigma_\beta
        =
        \rho_\beta^{Q_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_\beta^{Q_n}.
\end{equation}
Then \(\sigma_\beta\) is a Gaussian product state and
\begin{equation}
        0
        \le
        F_\beta(\sigma_\beta)-F_\beta(\rho_\beta)
        \le
        \sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}}
        =
        \sqrt{\frac{2\log_2 d_{\rm loc}}{D}} .
        \label{eq:fermionic-free-energy-product-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The lower bound follows from the Gibbs variational principle, since
\(\rho_\beta\) minimizes \(F_\beta\).
Thus, the nontrivial step is to prove the upper bound.  Let \(M^{(\beta)}\) be the covariance matrix of
\(\rho_\beta\).  For an oriented edge \((i,j)\in E\), set
\begin{equation}
        X_{i,j}^{(\beta)}
        :=
        \Pi_i M^{(\beta)}\Pi_j .
\end{equation}
As in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:fermionic-product-state-approximation}, the operator
normalization \(\|H_{i,j}\|\le1\) implies
\begin{equation}
        \|K_{i,j}\|_2\le1.
\end{equation}
Using the covariance convention \eqref{eq:majorana-covariance}, we have
\begin{equation}
        \tr(\rho_\beta H_{i,j})
        =
        -\tr\!\left(K_{i,j}^T X_{i,j}^{(\beta)}\right),
\end{equation}
and therefore
\begin{equation}
        \left|
        \tr\!\left(K_{i,j}^T X_{i,j}^{(\beta)}\right)
        \right|
        \le
        \|X_{i,j}^{(\beta)}\|_2 .
\end{equation}
Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:monogamy} at each vertex and averaging over the
edges gives
\begin{equation}
        \mathbb E_{(i,j)\in E}
        \left|
        \tr\!\left(K_{i,j}^T X_{i,j}^{(\beta)}\right)
        \right|
        \le
        \sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}} .
        \label{eq:gibbs-average-edge-bound}
\end{equation}

Now compare \(\rho_\beta\) with
\begin{equation}
        \sigma_\beta
        =
        \rho_\beta^{Q_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_\beta^{Q_n}.
\end{equation}
Passing from \(\rho_\beta\) to \(\sigma_\beta\) keeps the one-site marginals
and deletes the covariance blocks between distinct sites.  Therefore,
for every edge \((i,j)\in E\),
\begin{equation}
        \tr(\sigma_\beta H_{i,j})-\tr(\rho_\beta H_{i,j})
        =
        \tr\!\left(K_{i,j}^T X_{i,j}^{(\beta)}\right).
\end{equation}
Averaging over edges and using \eqref{eq:gibbs-average-edge-bound}, we obtain
\begin{equation}
        \tr(H\sigma_\beta)-\tr(H\rho_\beta)
        \le
        \sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}} .
\end{equation}

It remains to use the entropy term.  Since \(\sigma_\beta\) is the product of
the one-site marginals of \(\rho_\beta\), subadditivity gives
\begin{equation}
        S(\sigma_\beta)
        =
        \sum_{i=1}^n S(\rho_\beta^{Q_i})
        \ge
        S(\rho_\beta).
\end{equation}
Hence
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
        F_\beta(\sigma_\beta)-F_\beta(\rho_\beta)
        &=
        \tr(H\sigma_\beta)-\tr(H\rho_\beta)
        -
        \beta^{-1}\bigl(S(\sigma_\beta)-S(\rho_\beta)\bigr)  \\
        &\le
        \tr(H\sigma_\beta)-\tr(H\rho_\beta)  \\
        &\le
        \sqrt{\frac{2m}{D}} .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:fermionic-free-energy-product-bound}.
\end{proof}

\section{Exchangeability and fermionic Gaussian de Finetti bounds}
\label{sec:definetti}

We now turn to the role of exchangeability.  In ordinary quantum de Finetti
theory, permutation symmetry, together with extendibility to a sufficiently
large number of copies, leads to approximate product structure.  In the
fermionic Gaussian setting, this principle admits a particularly direct and
rigid formulation at the level of covariance matrices.  Graded permutation
symmetry forces all off-diagonal covariance blocks between distinct copies to
coincide, while the bona fide condition for the full \(n\)-copy covariance
matrix suppresses their magnitude to order \(1/n\).

The proof is entirely one-particle.  We first state the finite de Finetti
theorem.  We then write the exchangeable covariance matrix in block form and
diagonalize its copy-space part into the symmetric direction and its orthogonal
complement.  The two resulting one-copy covariance matrices differ by exactly
\(nY\), where \(Y\) is the common off-diagonal covariance block.  This gives the
covariance suppression bound, which is then converted into a trace-norm bound
between Gaussian states.

Let \(A\) be a fermionic system with \(m_A\) modes, equivalently \(N_A=2m_A\)
Majorana operators.  We write \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) for \(k\) identical copies of
\(A\), with the global ordering of copies fixed once and for all.
For \(\pi\in S_n\), let \(U_\pi\) be the graded fermionic copy-permutation
unitary determined by
\begin{equation}
        U_\pi^\dagger\gamma_a^{(i)}U_\pi
        =
        \gamma_a^{(\pi(i))}.
        \label{eq:graded-copy-permutation}
\end{equation}
All permutation invariance in this section refers to these fermionic
permutation unitaries, rather than to ordinary tensor-factor permutations
after a Jordan--Wigner identification.

\begin{definition}[\(n\)-exchangeability]
Let \(1\le k\le n\).  A state \(\rho_{A_1, \cdots , A_k}\) is called
\(n\)-exchangeable if there exists a physical state
\(\widetilde\rho_{A_1\cdots A_n}\) which satisfies
\(U_\pi\widetilde\rho U_\pi^\dagger=\widetilde\rho\) for every \(\pi\in S_n\)
and whose marginal on \(A_1\cdots A_k\) is
\(\rho_{A_1, \cdots , A_k}\).  A state is infinitely exchangeable if it is
\(n\)-exchangeable for every \(n\ge k\).
\end{definition}

The main result of this section is the following finite de Finetti bound.

\begin{theorem}[Finite fermionic Gaussian de Finetti bound]
\label{thm:exchangeable-gaussian-definetti}
Let \(\rho_{A_1, \cdots , A_k}\) be an \(n\)-exchangeable fermionic Gaussian state,
and let \(\rho_A\) be its one-copy marginal.  Then there exists a probability
measure \(\mu\) on the set of physical states of \(A\) such that
\begin{equation}
        \trnorm{
        \rho_{A_1, \cdots , A_k}
        -
        \int \omega^{\otimes k}\,d\mu(\omega)
        }
        \le
        \frac{4m_A(k-1)}{n}.
        \label{eq:finite-definetti-bound}
\end{equation}
In fact, one may take \(\mu=\delta_{\rho_A}\), so that the approximating
de Finetti state is simply \(\rho_A^{\otimes k}\).
\end{theorem}

The case \(k=1\) is immediate.  Hence, in the covariance analysis below, we
assume \(2\le k\le n\).
The remainder
of this section proves
Theorem~\ref{thm:exchangeable-gaussian-definetti}.  For fermionic Gaussian
states, exchangeability can be checked directly at the covariance level.
Given any permutation-invariant extension \(\widetilde\rho\), let
\(\widetilde M\) be its covariance matrix and let \(\rho_{\widetilde M}\) be
the unique Gaussian state with this covariance matrix.  The matrix
\(\widetilde M\) is permutation invariant, and uniqueness implies that
\(\rho_{\widetilde M}\) is permutation invariant as well.  Its \(k\)-copy
marginal has the covariance matrix of \(\rho_{A_1, \cdots , A_k}\); since the
prescribed marginal is Gaussian, uniqueness shows that this marginal of
\(\rho_{\widetilde M}\) is precisely \(\rho_{A_1, \cdots, A_k}\).  Thus an
arbitrary permutation-invariant extension may be replaced by a
permutation-invariant Gaussian extension with the same marginal.  Conversely, every admissible
permutation-invariant covariance extension determines such a Gaussian state
extension.

\subsection{Permutation-invariant covariance matrices}
\label{subsec:exchangeable-sector-suppression}

We now translate graded permutation symmetry into the rigid block
structure that drives the quantitative de Finetti bound.
Let \(\rho_{A_1, \cdots , A_k}\) be permutation-invariant and Gaussian, and let
\(M^{(k)}\) be its Majorana covariance matrix.  Since all copies are identical,
permutation invariance implies that all diagonal blocks are equal to the
one-copy covariance matrix \(M_A\), and that all off-diagonal copy-copy blocks
are described by a single matrix \(Y\).

There is one fermionic point to note.  A priori, the two-copy covariance matrix
has the block form
\begin{equation}
        \begin{pmatrix}
        M_A & Y\\
        -Y^T & M_A
        \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
However, for a permutation-invariant fermionic extension, the off-diagonal
block \(Y\) is itself antisymmetric.  Indeed, with the covariance convention
\begin{equation}
        M_{p,q}
        =
        \tr\!\left(i\gamma_q\gamma_p\rho\right)
        \qquad (p\ne q),
\end{equation}
we have
\begin{equation}
        Y_{A,B}
        =
        \tr\!\left(
        i\gamma^{(2)}_b\gamma^{(1)}_a\rho
        \right).
\end{equation}
Exchanging the two copies gives
\begin{equation}
        Y_{A,B}
        =
        \tr\!\left(
        i\gamma^{(1)}_b\gamma^{(2)}_a\rho
        \right)
        =
        -
        \tr\!\left(
        i\gamma^{(2)}_a\gamma^{(1)}_b\rho
        \right)
        =
        -Y_{b,a},
\end{equation}
where the minus sign comes from the canonical anticommutation relations for
Majorana operators on distinct fermionic copies.  Hence \(Y^T=-Y\).  This is
the covariance-matrix version of the antisymmetry condition for fermionic
symmetric extensions; see, for example, the covariance characterization of
fermionic extendibility in \citep{NegariSalekExtendibility}.  Consequently
\(-Y^T=Y\), and the permutation-invariant \(k\)-copy covariance matrix may be
written as
\begin{equation}
        M^{(k)}
        =
        \begin{pmatrix}
        M_A & Y & \cdots & Y\\
        Y & M_A & \cdots & Y\\
        \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
        Y & Y & \cdots & M_A
        \end{pmatrix}.
        \label{eq:exchangeable-block-matrix}
\end{equation}
Here both \(M_A\) and \(Y\) are real antisymmetric matrices.

The proof therefore reduces to showing that \(n\)-exchangeability forces
\(\trnorm{Y}=O(m_A/n)\).  Once this is known, the covariance matrix
\eqref{eq:exchangeable-block-matrix} is close to the product covariance
\(M_A^{\oplus k}\), and the covariance-to-state Lipschitz bound for fermionic
Gaussian states gives \eqref{eq:finite-definetti-bound}.

Let \(M^{(n)}\) be a permutation-invariant \(n\)-copy covariance matrix
extending \(M^{(k)}\).  Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
        M^{(n)}
        =
        \one_n\otimes M_A
        +
        (J_n-\one_n)\otimes Y,
\end{equation}
where \(J_n\) is the \(n\times n\) all-ones matrix and \(\one_n\) is the
\(n\times n\) identity.  Define
\begin{equation}
        \ket{+}
        :=
        \frac1{\sqrt n}(1,\ldots,1)^T,
        \qquad
        P_+:=\ket{+}\!\bra{+},
        \qquad
        P_-:=\one_n-P_+ .
\end{equation}
The vector \(\ket{+}\) spans the symmetric copy-space sector.  Since
\(J_n-\one_n\) has eigenvalue \(n-1\) on this sector and eigenvalue \(-1\) on
its orthogonal complement, the covariance matrix decomposes as
\begin{equation}
        M^{(n)}
        =
        P_+\otimes\bigl(M_A+(n-1)Y\bigr)
        +
        P_-\otimes(M_A-Y).
        \label{eq:exchangeable-sector-decomposition}
\end{equation}
Thus the \(n\)-copy bona fide condition reduces to two one-copy bona fide
conditions.

**TL;DR** The authors observe that the bona-fide condition for Majorana covariance matrices ($\mathbb{1}+iM\succeq 0$, hence $MM^T\preceq\mathbb{1}$) immediately implies a sharp "covariance monogamy" bound: for a region $A$ correlated with disjoint regions $B_1,\dots,B_k$, the cross blocks obey $\sum_i X_iX_i^T\preceq\mathbb{1}_A$, so the average $\|X_i\|_2^2\le 2m_A/k$. From this one-particle inequality alone they derive (i) a $\sqrt{2m/D}$ product-state approximation to ground-state energy and free energy of quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians on $D$-regular graphs, (ii) a finite Gaussian de Finetti bound $\|\rho_{A_1\cdots A_k}-\rho_A^{\otimes k}\|_1\le 4m_A(k-1)/n$, and (iii) $O(1/r)$ decay of conditional mutual information across a buffer, hence $O(r^{-1/2})$ recoverability.

**The big picture** A long-standing intuition in many-body physics is that when a degree of freedom is coupled to very many others, or when a state is symmetric under swapping many identical copies, the system behaves as if it had no correlations at all — mean-field theory becomes accurate. For free-fermion systems, all correlations live in a single matrix of two-point functions, and the mere requirement that such a matrix come from a genuine quantum state already caps how much correlation one region can share with many others. The paper shows that this elementary constraint, used directly, reproduces and sharpens three otherwise unrelated approximation theorems — mean-field energy bounds, de Finetti theorems, and approximate conditional independence across a spatial buffer — with short proofs and better rates.

**Key contributions**
- A sharp monogamy inequality for fermionic two-point functions, valid for arbitrary (non-Gaussian) physical states, with a saturating example for every $k$.
- Product-state energy bound $e_0(H)+\sqrt{2\log_2 d_{\rm loc}/D}$, improving Brandão–Harrow's $(d_{\rm loc}^2\log d_{\rm loc}/D)^{1/3}$ to $D^{-1/2}$ with only polylogarithmic local-dimension dependence; approximant can be taken pure and a parity eigenstate; extends to arbitrary (non-quadratic) even on-site terms.
- A finite-temperature analogue: the product of one-site Gibbs marginals is within $\sqrt{2m/D}$ of the free-energy optimum.
- A covariance-level fermionic de Finetti theorem whose limiting measure is a *point mass* — infinite exchangeability within the Gaussian class implies exact product structure.
- CMI bound $I(A:C|B_r)\le K/r$ for spatially clustering Gaussian states, plus Fawzi–Renner recoverability.

**How it works** Edge energies of a quadratic Hamiltonian are exactly linear in the covariance block, $\mathrm{tr}(\rho H_{ij})=-\mathrm{tr}(K_{ij}^TX_{ij})$, with $\|K_{ij}\|_1=\|H_{ij}\|\le1$; Cauchy–Schwarz plus monogamy and Jensen bound the average edge error. For de Finetti, graded copy-permutation symmetry forces all off-diagonal blocks equal and *antisymmetric*, so $M^{(n)}=P_+\otimes(M_A+(n-1)Y)+P_-\otimes(M_A-Y)$; admissibility of both sectors forces $\|Y\|_1=O(m_A/n)$, converted to trace distance via $\|\rho_M-\rho_{M'}\|_1\le\frac12\|M-M'\|_1$. The CMI result expands Gaussian entropies as traces of compressed Green operators and sums Green-function paths crossing the buffer.

**Why it matters** Clean, optimal-constant benchmarks for mean-field accuracy and extendibility hierarchies in free-fermion systems; relevant to Hartree–Fock-type variational bounds, matchgate/fermionic shadow tomography, and entanglement-of-modes theory under parity superselection.

**Caveats** The de Finetti theorem assumes the joint state is Gaussian and permutation-symmetrically extendible — strictly narrower than quantum de Finetti, which is what buys the point-mass conclusion. Product/separability notions are tied to a fixed mode partition and global ordering. The free-energy bound simply discards the entropy difference, so it is $\beta$-independent and presumably loose at high temperature. Most strikingly, exponentially clustering mutual information yields only $1/r$ CMI decay; whether the path expansion can be improved to exponential (as in recent Gibbs-state results) is left open. All statements are finite-mode; the thermodynamic/continuum limits are not treated.
